Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Here’s a simple overview of your main choices when you’re starting with roses from us:

Where the rose will live
In the ground: Best long-term choice if you have a garden bed.
In a large pot: Works well if you have a patio, balcony, or poor soil. You’ll just need a big container and good potting soil.
How big you want it to get
Bush/Shrub roses: Rounded plants, usually 3–5 feet tall. Great for most gardens and beginners.
Climbing roses: Long canes that you tie to a trellis, fence, or arbor. Beautiful for vertical spaces, but need a support.
Groundcover roses (low, spreading): Stay low and spread out, good for the front of beds or along edges.
Flower style
Big, classic “long-stem” type blooms: Often hybrid tea or similar; great for cutting and vases.
Clusters of many blooms: More flowers at once, very showy in the garden.
Old-fashioned/romantic blooms: Many petals, cupped or rosette shapes, very full-looking.
Bloom habit
Repeat/continuous blooming: Flower, rest, flower again through the season. Easiest for lots of color.
Fragrance
Strongly fragrant: Amazing smell, perfect if scent is important to you.
Lightly fragrant or nearly none: Better if you’re sensitive to scents.
Color
You can pretty much pick any color: pinks, reds, whites, yellows, apricots, purples, and blends.
Sun and climate
Sun: Roses need at least 6 hours of direct sun a day.
Climate: On our site you can choose your hardiness zone at the top so you only see roses that are suited to your area.

And a quick note about our plants:

All our roses are own-root and come in 1-gallon containers with soil (not bare root), ready to plant.

Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You’re asking all the right questions. Here’s what most beginners find helpful to have on hand.

1) Soil amendments (optional but very helpful) These mix into your planting hole or go around the plant to improve the soil:

Bone meal: Helps strong root growth, especially at planting.
Cow manure (aged/composted): Adds long‑lasting nutrients and improves soil structure.
Mint compost: Lightens and aerates the soil and can also be used as a gentle top layer to protect roots.
Worm castings: Very gentle nutrient boost and improves soil aeration and water holding.

You don’t have to use these, but they give your new rose a really good start. If you like simple, our all‑in‑one Get Growing Bundle has bone meal, mint compost, cow manure, and Founders Fish Fertilizer sized for 1–15 roses depending on the bundle you choose.

2) Fertilizer (needed for ongoing health) Roses do need regular feeding for strong growth and good blooms.

We offer fertilizers like OmniMeal and Founders Fish Fertilizer.
You can use any good rose fertilizer you prefer.
For the first year, a liquid fertilizer is often easiest because it’s gentle and easy to apply with water.

3) Simple basics you’ll also want

A spot with at least 6 hours of sun.
Good drainage so water doesn’t sit around the roots.
A watering plan (deep, regular watering, especially the first season).

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question; using it right the first time makes a big difference.

I’ll explain as if you’re using our Get Growing Bundle (cow manure, bone meal, mint compost, and Founders Fish Fertilizer). If you only have some of these, just use the parts that apply.

If you’re planting in the ground

Step 1: Prepare the hole

Dig a hole about 2 feet wide and deep.
Loosen the surrounding soil so roots can spread.

Step 2: Mix in amendments In a bucket or wheelbarrow, mix your existing soil with:

Cow manure: This is your long-term food source. Mix some into the soil that will go back into the hole.
Bone meal: Add about 1 cup into that soil mix to support root growth.
Mint compost: Mix in roughly one small bag per rose (if you have the bundle) or a few generous scoops. This improves drainage and water holding.

Put a couple of inches of this amended soil in the bottom of the hole.

Step 3: Plant the rose

Take the rose out of its 1-gallon container and gently loosen the outer roots.
Set it in the hole so the base of the plant is level with the surrounding ground.
Backfill with your soil + amendment mix.
Press gently to remove air pockets.

Step 4: Water and fertilize

Water deeply so all the soil settles and is evenly moist, not soggy.
Mix Founders Fish Fertilizer at 4 oz per gallon of water.
Water the rose with this mixture at planting.

After that, in the ground use:

Founders Fish Fertilizer every 4–6 weeks during the growing season.
Mint compost as a light top layer around the plant every 6 months.
If you’re planting in a container

Step 1: Prepare the pot

Choose a large container with drainage holes.
Fill with good quality potting soil (no granular or time-release fertilizer added).

Step 2: Mix in amendments

Cow manure: Mix some into the potting soil before planting.
Bone meal: Mix about 1 cup into the potting soil.

Step 3: Plant the rose

Place some of the amended soil in the bottom of the pot.
Set the rose in so the base is at soil level.
Fill around it with the amended soil and press gently.

Step 4: Top dress and fertilize

Mint compost: Spread a thin layer on top of the soil around the base of the plant.
Water thoroughly.
Mix Founders Fish Fertilizer at 4 oz per gallon of water and water the plant with this.

After that, in a pot use:

Founders Fish Fertilizer every 3–4 weeks.
Refresh the mint compost top layer about every 6 months.
